title: Forward design of thick Fe–N–C cathodes  via  decoupled self-humidification and anti-flooding
content: Fe–N–C catalysts are promising non-platinum-group metal alternatives for proton exchange membrane fuel cells; however, the requisite thick cathode catalyst layers (CCLs) elongate proton-conduction pathways and aggravate liquid-water accumulation, imposing stringent water-management constraints. Here, we develop a quantitative structure–water-management–performance framework by integrating electrochemical characterization with three-dimensional, two-phase, non-isothermal simulations. We identify intra-CCL H+ and O2 transport resistances, rather than intrinsic oxygen reduction kinetics, as the primary architecture-dependent bottlenecks. Mechanistic analysis indicates that self-humidification and anti-flooding are coupled but non-equivalent objectives that follow a volcano-type balance, defining an explicit trade-off for cathode-architecture design. Guided by this principle, a dam-inspired grooved CCL spatially decouples local water retention from liquid-water removal. Gaussian process regression with Bayesian optimization yields a voltage-resolved rule: the optimal groove ratio decreases from 3.96 (high-voltage) to 3.67 (mid-voltage) and 3.30 (low-voltage). Grooved cathodes fabricated at the predicted ratios reproduce this voltage-dependent rule experimentally, and the ranking is retained after 30 000 accelerated-stress-test cycles; a grooved CCL with a 3 : 1 ratio delivers a peak power density approximately 50% higher than the conventional CCL (0.62 versus 0.41 W cm−2 under H2–air). These findings establish a forward-design framework for thick Fe–N–C cathodes, extendable to porous electrochemical electrodes.
